When the digit to be dropped is **exactly 5**, the convention is to round so that the
preceding digit becomes **even**.
**Step 1 — state the rule.** If the digit dropped is 5 with nothing after it:
if the preceding digit is **even**, leave it unchanged
if the preceding digit is **odd**, raise it by one ✓
This is the "round half to even" rule used throughout physics.
**Step 2 — apply it to 2·745.** The digit to be dropped is 5; the preceding digit is
**4, which is even**, so it stays:
2·745 → **2·74** ✓
**Step 3 — apply it to 2·735.** The digit to be dropped is 5; the preceding digit is
**3, which is odd**, so it is raised to 4:
2·735 → **2·74** ✓
**Step 4 — read the pair.** Both round to **2·74 and 2·74** ✓
**Why the rule exists.** Always rounding 5 upward would bias a long series of
measurements **high** ✓ Rounding half the cases up and half down - which is what the
even rule does, since odd and even preceding digits occur about equally - leaves the
average unbiased. Over thousands of readings that matters.
**A check across a run of numbers.**
2·715 → **2·72** (1 odd, up)
2·725 → **2·72** (2 even, stays)
2·735 → **2·74** (3 odd, up)
2·745 → **2·74** (4 even, stays) ✓
The results alternate, so the upward and downward roundings balance exactly.
**What the rule does not cover.** If anything follows the 5, ordinary rounding applies:
2·7451 → **2·75**, because the part being dropped is now clearly more than half ✓ The
even rule is only for the exact halfway case.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·75 and 2·74** ✗ rounds the first up, ignoring that 4 is
even. **2·74 and 2·73** ✗ rounds the second down, though 3 is odd. **2·75 and 2·73** ✗
gets both wrong ✓
∴ 2·74 and 2·74.

Compute the area, round it by the significant-figure rule, then propagate the errors.
**Step 1 — multiply.**
A = 16·2 x 10·1
= **163·62 cm²**
**Step 2 — round to the right number of significant figures.** Both measurements have
**three** significant figures, so the area must too:
**A = 164 cm²** ✓
**Step 3 — find the uncertainty in each measurement.** A reading of 16·2 cm is good to
the last digit quoted, so Δl = **0·1 cm**, and likewise Δb = **0·1 cm**.
**Step 4 — add the fractional errors.** For a product, relative errors add:
ΔA/A = Δl/l + Δb/b
= 0·1/16·2 + 0·1/10·1
= 0·00617 + 0·00990
= **0·01607**, about **1·6%**
**Step 5 — convert to an absolute error.**
ΔA = 0·01607 x 163·62
= 2·63
≈ **3 cm²** ✓
**Step 6 — state the result consistently.**
**A = 164 ± 3 cm²** ✓
**Why the error is rounded to one figure.** An uncertainty is itself an estimate, and
quoting it as 2·63 cm² claims a precision the estimate does not have ✓ One significant
figure is standard practice.
**Why the value must then stop at the units place.** With an uncertainty of ±3 cm², the
digits after the decimal point in 163·62 are meaningless ✓ The value and its error must
be quoted to the **same** decimal place - which is why 163·62 ± 3 cm² is internally
inconsistent, and why the answer is 164 ± 3.
**Reading the distractors.** **163·62 ± 2·6 cm²** ✗ and **163·6 ± 2·6 cm²** ✗ keep more
figures in the value than the error permits. **163·62 ± 3 cm²** ✗ pairs a two-decimal
value with a whole-number error ✓ Only one option is consistent in both respects.
∴ 164 ± 3 cm².

Check each pair in turn; three match and one does not.
**Work and torque** - both are **force x distance**:
work: [M L² T⁻²] (joule)
torque: [M L² T⁻²] (newton metre) ✓ **same**
They differ in nature - work is a scalar, torque a vector - but their dimensions are
identical.
**Angular momentum and Planck's constant** -
angular momentum L = mvr: [M][L T⁻¹][L] = **[M L² T⁻¹]**
Planck's constant, from E = hν: [M L² T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = **[M L² T⁻¹]** ✓ **same**
This is why ℏ is called the **quantum of angular momentum**, and why angular momentum in
quantum mechanics comes in units of ℏ.
**Impulse and linear momentum** -
impulse = FΔt: [M L T⁻²][T] = **[M L T⁻¹]**
momentum = mv: **[M L T⁻¹]** ✓ **same**
and necessarily so, since the impulse-momentum theorem states that one **equals** the
other.
**Tension and surface tension** -
tension is a **force**: [M L T⁻²], measured in **newtons**
surface tension is force **per unit length**: [M T⁻²], measured in **N m⁻¹** ✓
**different** - they differ by one power of length.
**Step — identify the odd pair.** Only tension and surface tension fail to match ✓
**Why the names mislead.** "Surface tension" sounds like a kind of tension, but it is
defined as the force acting per unit length of a line drawn in the surface, or
equivalently as **energy per unit area** ✓ Both readings give [M T⁻²]:
energy/area = [M L² T⁻²]/[L²] = **[M T⁻²]** ✓ consistent.
**The lesson.** Dimensional identity does not imply physical identity - work and torque
share dimensions but are quite different quantities ✓ And similar **names** are no guide
at all, as this pair shows.
**Typical values.** Water has a surface tension of about **0·072 N m⁻¹**; a rope might
carry a tension of **100 N** ✓ The units themselves announce the difference.
∴ tension and surface tension.

Write out the dimensions of each symbol and see what survives.
**Step 1 — list the dimensions.**
E, energy: **[M L² T⁻²]**
m, mass: **[M]**
L, angular momentum: **[M L² T⁻¹]**
G, gravitational constant, from F = Gm₁m₂/r²: **[M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]**
**Step 2 — build the numerator, EL².**
E L² = [M L² T⁻²][M L² T⁻¹]²
= [M L² T⁻²][M² L⁴ T⁻²]
= **[M³ L⁶ T⁻⁴]**
**Step 3 — build the denominator, m⁵G².**
m⁵ G² = [M⁵][M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]²
= [M⁵][M⁻² L⁶ T⁻⁴]
= **[M³ L⁶ T⁻⁴]**
**Step 4 — divide.**
EL²/(m⁵G²) = [M³ L⁶ T⁻⁴]/[M³ L⁶ T⁻⁴]
= **[M⁰ L⁰ T⁰]** - dimensionless ✓
**Step 5 — choose among the options.** Of the four, only **angle** is dimensionless ✓
Length, mass and time each carry a dimension, so none can match.
**Checking the dimensions of G.** From F = Gm₁m₂/r²:
[G] = [F][L²]/[M²] = [M L T⁻²][L²]/[M²] = **[M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]** ✓ and its SI unit,
N m² kg⁻², says the same thing.
**Why "dimensionless" does not mean "unitless".** Angle is measured in **radians**, yet
it is the ratio of two lengths and so carries no dimensions ✓ The radian is a unit
without a dimension - which is exactly why it is the right answer here.
**Other dimensionless quantities.** Strain, refractive index, relative density, the
Reynolds number and the fine-structure constant ✓ Any of them would fit the dimensions;
"angle" is the one offered.
**Why combinations like this are built.** Dimensionless groups are the basis of
**dimensional analysis** - they are what remains when all the units have been divided
out, and they govern the behaviour of a system independently of the units chosen ✓
∴ angle.
